meta.obligation: Preserve/demonstrate that Restart's wait-for-live logic must not hold the agent's internal state mutex for the duration of waitUntilLive, so that a concurrently exiting epoch can still be processed by Run (via a.mutex) and the waiting Restart can detect the epoch's exit (via isActive) and proceed promptly, rather than deadlocking until the 20s timeout.
meta.rationale:
The supplied test TestExitDuringWaitForLive (shared/pkg/envoy/agent_test.go:169-221) already exercises exactly the behavior changed by the diff: it starts epoch 0 (which never goes live), immediately calls Restart for epoch 1 in a goroutine (which must wait for epoch 0's liveness per agent.go Restart/waitUntilLive), then delivers an exit error for epoch 0 via epoch0Exit and asserts (with a 5s bound and a BeTemporally ~1s threshold) that epoch 1 starts promptly rather than after the full 20s live-wait timeout.

In the defective version, Restart holds the single a.mu for the entire Restart call including the blocking waitUntilLive (agent.go:125-136 old), and Run's status-handling branch also needs a.mu (agent.go:193) to delete the exited epoch from activeEpochs. Since waitUntilLive only re-checks proxy.IsLive() (never true here) and does not release the lock, Run can never process epoch 0's exit status, so waitUntilLive can only end via its own 20s timer — well past the test's 5s bound. Paired execution confirms this: the defective run blocks and fails with `agent_test.go:213: timed out waiting for epoch 1 to start`, with goroutine dump showing goroutine 7 stuck in `waitUntilLive` (agent.go:175) inside `Restart` (agent.go:136), and goroutine 5 blocked trying to acquire the same mutex in `Run` (agent.go:193).

In the repaired version, Restart releases a.mutex before waiting (agent.go new Restart, `a.mutex.Unlock()` before wait) and waitUntilLive additionally polls `isActive(epoch)` (agent.go new isActive, guarded by a.mutex) so it can detect that epoch 0 exited (processed promptly by Run under the now-available mutex) and return quickly. Paired execution confirms this: the repaired run logs "epoch 0 exited while waiting for it to go live." and epoch 1 starts within ~0.5s, and the test PASSes.

This paired run result (defective FAIL via timeout/goroutine-dump showing the lock contention, repaired PASS quickly) is direct evidence that the existing unmodified test already discriminates the changed obligation (lock-scope/liveness-wait interaction between Restart and Run), so no overlay edit is needed.</rationale>

meta.obligation: pop() must not hold p.lock while blocked sending a notification on p.nextCh, so that concurrent callers (e.g. add()) can still acquire the lock during a blocked send.
meta.rationale: The production diff narrows the lock scope in (processorListener).pop: originally p.lock was held for the entire loop body including the blocking send on p.nextCh (defective/shared_informer.go:282-303); the repair moves the lock/unlock into a `blockingGet` closure that only covers the pendingNotifications dequeue, releasing the lock before the blocking select on p.nextCh/stopCh (repaired diff lines 281-305). The supplied test TestPopReleaseLock (processor_listener_test.go:28-48) exactly targets this obligation: it calls pl.add(1) then runs pl.pop(stopCh) in a goroutine, which blocks on the p.nextCh send since no receiver drains it; concurrently it spawns a goroutine trying to pl.lock.Lock(). If pop() held the lock during the blocked send (defective), the second goroutine's Lock() would never succeed, resultCh would never close, and the test times out via time.After(wait.ForeverTestTimeout) with t.Errorf. If pop() releases the lock before blocking on the send (repaired), the lock acquisition succeeds promptly and the test passes quickly. This is a direct, minimal, already-present witness of the exact changed lock-scoping behavior; the T0 extraction also ranks it top overlap (score=9) with the changed function. No modification improves on this: the test's core structure already isolates the lock-release timing without relying on t.Errorf failure text or timeout duration changes, so I retain it unmodified.

There is a small chance GOMAXPROCS=16 scheduling makes the defective variant's failure intermittent rather than deterministic, though the blocking design (cond.Wait/select with no receiver) should make it deterministic within the ForeverTestTimeout window.
